query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing high‐entropy alloying by multi‐element doping into ZrB2 to form a single-phase high‐entropy metal diboride will allow synthesis at lower temperatures (∼1700 °C) while simultaneously enhancing its strength, oxidation durability, and liquid plating‐metal corrosion resistance compared to both conventional high‐temperature (>2300 °C) ZrB2 and other lower‐temperature specimens.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase ZrB2 prepared by high-temperature sintering (>2300 °C), which exhibits strong Zr–B and B–B interactions but requires high processing temperatures.
generation.intervention: High‐entropy alloying via multi‐element doping of ZrB2; for example, synthesizing a composition such as (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2 using high-energy ball milling (HEBM) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) at reduced temperatures (∼1700 °C).
generation.conditions: Fabrication by HEBM and SPS at temperatures near or below 1700 °C; service conditions involving high-temperature oxidation environments (up to ∼1500 °C in air) and exposure to liquid plating-metal baths.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a single-phase, high-entropy solid-solution diboride where the uniform dispersion of multiple metal cations reduces defects and phase boundaries, thereby stabilizing the diboride lattice at lower sintering temperatures.
generation.mechanism: The increased configurational entropy from multi-element doping lowers the energy barrier for densification, promotes single-phase formation at reduced temperatures, and improves microstructural uniformity. This in turn enhances mechanical hardness and resistance to oxidation and corrosive liquid-metal environments by eliminating weak points and reducing oxidation-prone intermetallic boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: The high‐entropy metal diboride will exhibit a higher hardness, improved oxidation resistance, and better liquid-metal corrosion performance compared to conventional single-phase ZrB2 synthesized at >2300 °C and lower-temperature specimens, while being manufacturable at ~1700 °C.
generation.baseline: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 synthesized at >2300 °C and lower-temperature specimens (∼1700 °C) that suffer from multiphase formation or compromised oxidation and corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective provided that the elemental size disparity (δ) remains below approximately 3.9% to ensure a stable single phase. Service temperatures should be maintained near or below 1500 °C for optimal performance.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the exact composition window and the quantitative magnitude of improvements in mechanical and corrosion properties, which will depend on the precise dopant levels and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of specimens using HEBM and SPS with varying compositions around (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2 at sintering temperatures at or below 1700 °C. Characterize the phase purity using X-ray diffraction, evaluate the microstructure via SEM/TEM, and measure the Vickers hardness. Conduct oxidation tests under flowing dry air at increasing temperatures up to 1500 °C and perform liquid-metal plating corrosion experiments in a controlled bath.
measurements: Oxidation resistance (weight gain/loss and structural integrity after high-temperature exposure)
Liquid-metal corrosion resistance (post-exposure mechanical and microstructural assessment)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the synthesized high-entropy metal diboride specimen either displays multiphase regions (i.e., fails to form a single-phase solid solution) or does not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in hardness, oxidation resistance, and corrosion resistance compared to the conventional high-temperature ZrB2 or lower-temperature specimens, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To investigate the correlation between the size difference factor (δ) and the phase composition of the samples, we performed XRD analysis on six different high-entropy borides. The results are presented in Figure 2. From the graph, it is evident that (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Mo)B2, and (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta, Mo)B2 all exhibit a single-phase structure, with their respective lattice parameters listed in Table 1. In contrast, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Ta, W)B2 and (Ti, Zr, Hf, Mo, W)B2 show variations. In the XRD patterns of (Ti, Zr, Hf, Ta, W)B2 and (Ti, Zr, Hf, Mo, W)B2 systems, in addition to the high-entropy phase, impurity phases such as (Mo, W)2B5, W2B5, and minor amounts of (Ti, Zr, Hf, Mo, W)C and B4C were observed. Notably, these non-single-phase (Ti, Zr, Hf, Ta, W)B2 and (Ti, Zr, Hf, Mo, W)B2 systems corresponded to higher δ values. Hence, it is less likely to form single-phase, high-entropy borides when δ exceeds 3.9%. In the upcoming experiments, our focus will be on (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2, which boasts the smallest δ value.

Initial property assessments indicated that both the hardness and the oxidation resistance of these high-entropy metal diborides are generally greater or better than the average performances of the individual (conventional) metal diborides made by the identical HEBM and SPS fabrication processing. We understand that both hardness and oxidation resistance should critically depend on microstructures; the presence of porosity and oxide inclusion, as a consequence of the HEBM procedure that we adopted for promoting the homogenization of high-entropy solid solutions, adversely affected the hardness and oxidation resistance. It is worth making a few additional notes regarding the observed phase stabilities. First, perhaps the most interesting observation is the formation of a single-phase, high-entropy solution in HEB #7, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ti0.2Cr0.2Ta0.2)B2, despite the limited solid solubilities of CrB2 in both HfB2 and ZrB2,. Second, MoB2 is believed to be metastable at room temperature, but the hexagonal MoB2 phase could be retained in the SPS specimens; in this study, four 20%-Mo-containing high-entropy metal diborides have been made. Third, the starting powder W2B5 (since WB2 is not commercially available) possessed a different structure and it has limited solubilities in all diborides except for TiB2,,, which can be another reason that HEB #6 did not possess a single solid-solution phase (in addition to the largest δc of ~6.2%). It is important to emphasize that both the hardness and oxidation resistance can be affected by the microstructure, e.g., the porosity and oxide inclusions, significantly. Hardness and oxidation measurements were conducted using all six single-phase high-entropy diborides (HEB #1-#5 and #7) and six individual metal diboride benchmarking specimens (HfB2, ZrB2, TaB2, NbB2, TiB2, and CrB2) that were made by the same HEBM and SPS fabrication method using the same processing parameters, with one exception that CrB2 was sintered at lower temperature of 1800 °C because its substantially lower melting (and therefore sintering) temperature. MoB2 was not examined because it is not a thermodynamically stable phase (and will decompose to MoB and Mo2B5) below 1500 °C. Hardness measurements were performed with a Vickers’ diamond indenter at 200 kgf/mm2 with a hold time of 15 seconds. The indentations were examined for conformation with the ASTM C1327. The indentations averaged 20–25 μm in width during the testing. Multiple measurements were performed at different locations of each specimen; the mean and standard deviation are reported.
